claims.claim: There is substantial contralateral symmetry regarding the relative contribution and areal identity of input to VISp, SSp-bfd, and MOp.
claims.source: We find that although the ipsilateral hemisphere is the primary source of cortical input, there is substantial contralateral symmetry regarding the relative contribution and areal identity of input.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis showing strong relationships between ipsilateral and contralateral fractional counts (R2 values of 0.74, 0.64, and 0.83 for VISp, SSp-bfd, and MOp respectively).

claims.claim: Excitatory Layer 6 corticocortical cells (L6 CCs) are a major projection pathway within and between the two hemispheres.
claims.source: Laminar analysis of these input areas show that excitatory Layer 6 corticocortical cells (L6 CCs) are a major projection pathway within and between the two hemispheres.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by laminar analysis data showing L6 dominance in projections to primary sensory and motor areas.

claims.claim: Contra-hemispheric projections reflect a dominant feedback organization compared to their ipsi-cortical counterpart.
claims.source: Analysis of the relative contribution of inputs from supra- (feedforward) and infragranular (feedback) layers reveals that contra-hemispheric projections reflect a dominant feedback organization compared to their ipsi-cortical counterpart.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by fILN analysis showing higher values for contralateral compared to ipsilateral projections across all target areas.

claims.claim: The magnitude of the interhemispheric difference in hierarchy was largest for sensory and motor projection areas compared to frontal, medial, or lateral brain areas due to a proportional increase in input from L6 neurons.
claims.source: The magnitude of the interhemispheric difference in hierarchy was largest for sensory and motor projection areas compared to frontal, medial, or lateral brain areas due to a proportional increase in input from L6 neurons.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data showing that sensory-motor modules have significantly larger differences in fILN between hemispheres compared to prefrontal-medial-lateral modules, driven by increased L6 contributions.

claims.claim: The vast majority of neurons (>99%) projecting to all target areas were non-overlapping with GAD-expressing cells.
claims.source: We found that the vast majority of neurons (>99%) projecting to all target areas were non-overlapping with GAD-expressing cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 4A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by confocal imaging data showing minimal overlap between retrogradely labeled cells and GAD+ interneurons.

claims.claim: L6 projection neurons were non-overlapping with NTSR1-expressing L6 corticothalamic cells and therefore indicative of Layer 6 corticocortical cells (L6 CCs).
claims.source: Regarding L6 projection neurons, they were also found to be non-overlapping with NTSR1-expressing L6 corticothalamic cells and therefore indicative of Layer 6 corticocortical cells (L6 CCs) (Figure 1—figure supplement 4B, C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by confocal imaging data showing no overlap between retrogradely labeled cells and NTSR1+ cells in L6.

claims.claim: All three target areas received ipsilateral input from almost all cortical areas.
claims.source: While all three target areas received ipsilateral input from almost all cortical areas (VISp, range: 41–44, n = 6; SSp-bfd, range: 43–44, n = 6, MOp, range: 33–39, n = 6, Figure 1D)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by cell counting data showing the number of cortical areas containing labeled neurons for each target area.

claims.claim: The two sensory cortical targets received input on average from more areas than the primary motor cortex.
claims.source: the two sensory cortical targets received input on average from more areas than the primary motor cortex (Figure 1D, sensory = 43.58 ± 0.26, n = 12 vs. motor 36.67 ± 0.99, n = 6; p < 0.001, two-sided Wilcoxon rank-sum test).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical comparison of the number of input areas between sensory and motor targets.

claims.claim: There was no instance where a projection area in the contralateral hemisphere did not have an ipsilateral counterpart.
claims.source: Importantly, we found there to be no instance where a projection area in the contralateral hemisphere did not have an ipsilateral counterpart.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on analysis of the distribution of projection neurons across all cortical areas in both hemispheres.

claims.claim: There is a strong correlation between the fractional count of neurons in a given ipsilateral brain area with its contralateral counterpart for VISp (R2 = 0.74 ± 0.02), SSp-bfd (R2 = 0.64 ± 0.1), and MOp (R2 = 0.83 ± 0.03).
claims.source: we found a strong correlation between the fractional count of neurons in a given ipsilateral brain area with its contralateral counterpart (VISp R2 = 0.74 ± 0.02, p < 0.05; SSp-bfd R2 = 0.64 ± 0.1, p < 0.05; MOp R2 = 0.83 ± 0.03, p < 0.05, linear regression fit, Figure 1E, F).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by linear regression analysis of fractional cell counts between hemispheres.

claims.claim: 33/40 (VISp), 44/44 (SSp-bfd), and 29/33 (MOp) cortical areas showed no significant difference in relative projection weights between hemispheres.
claims.source: When directly comparing the within hemisphere relative projection weights of the individual cortical areas across the two hemispheres, we found that 33/40 (VISp), 44/44 (SSp-bfd), and 29/33 (MOp) were not significantly different from one another which indicates significant bilateral symmetry in the relative contribution of a given area to its hemispheric projectome (Figure 1G, individual one-sample t-tests on contra–ipsi difference, Bonferroni multiple comparison correction).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical testing comparing projection weights between hemispheres for individual cortical areas.

claims.claim: The mouse neocortex consists of six anatomical modules: prefrontal, lateral, somatomotor, visual, medial, and auditory.
claims.source: Based on their degree of inter-areal cortical connectivity it has been suggested that the mouse neocortex consists of six anatomical modules referred to as prefrontal, lateral, somatomotor, visual, medial, and auditory (Figure 2A, Harris et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on prior anatomical studies of cortical connectivity patterns.

claims.claim: The VISp projection was heavily dominated by input from the visual module.
claims.source: First, while the VISp projection was heavily dominated by input from the visual module (Figure 2B, ipsilateral visual module fractional count 0.42 ± 0.02 vs. lateral module 0.19 ± 0.02; contralateral visual module 0.42 ± 0.03 vs. lateral module 0.22 ± 0.02, p < 0.001, two-sided unpaired t-test)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of fractional cell counts by module with statistical comparison.

claims.claim: Both SSp-bfd and MOp targets received input predominantly from the somatomotor module.
claims.source: both the SSp-bfd and MOp targets received input predominantly from the somatomotor module (Figure 2B, SSp-bfd: ipsilateral somatomotor module fractional count 0.62 ± 0.05 vs. visual module 0.16 ± 0.03, contralateral somatomotor module 0.53 ± 0.02 vs. lateral module 0.24 ± 0.02, p < 0.001; MOp: ipsilateral somatomotor module 0.83 ± 0.02 vs. lateral module 0.08 ± 0.01, contralateral somatomotor module 0.71 ± 0.03 vs. lateral module 0.14 ± 0.01, p < 0.001, two-sided unpaired t-test).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of fractional cell counts by module with statistical comparison.

claims.claim: MOp received almost no input from the visual, auditory, and medial modules in either hemisphere (less than 0.01 fractional count for each of these three modules).
claims.source: Second, although both VISp and SSp-bfd received significant input from all modules in both hemispheres, we find there to be almost no input onto MOp from the visual, auditory, and medial modules in either hemisphere (Figure 2B, less than 0.01 fractional count for each of these three modules).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of fractional cell counts showing minimal input from specific modules to MOp.

claims.claim: The lateral module in the contralateral hemisphere projecting to VISp is more strongly weighted than its ipsilateral counterpart, driven primarily by the connection from the temporal association area (TEa) and ectorhinal cortex (ECT).
claims.source: For example, we find that the lateral module in the contralateral hemisphere projecting to VISp is more strongly weighted than its ipsilateral counterpart and that this is driven primarily by the connection from the temporal association area (TEa) and ectorhinal cortex (ECT) (Figure 2B, C, lateral module ipsilateral 0.19 ± 0.02 vs. contralateral 0.22 ± 0.02, p = 0.05, one-tailed paired t-test).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical comparison of lateral module contributions between hemispheres and analysis of individual area contributions.

claims.claim: The majority of detected neurons were located in L2/3, L5, and L6a with a very low fraction of labeled neurons in L4 and L6b.
claims.source: First, for each injection target we find that the majority of detected neurons were located in L2/3, L5, and L6a (Figure 3B) with a very low fraction of labeled neurons in L4 and L6b.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of the laminar distribution of labeled neurons across all cortical areas.

claims.claim: L2/3 was not the dominant layer of inter-areal input regardless of hemisphere.
claims.source: Regardless of hemisphere, L2/3 was found not to be the dominant layer of inter-areal input (Figure 3C1, C2, D1, D2).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of laminar dominance patterns across cortical areas and hemispheres.

claims.claim: For VISp and MOp, L6 dominated both the intra- and interhemispheric projection.
claims.source: For VISp and MOp L6 dominated both the intra- and interhemispheric projection (Figure 3C1, C2, D1, D2, p < 0.01, one-way ANOVA, Tukey–Kramer multiple comparison correction).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of laminar dominance patterns with multiple comparison correction.

claims.claim: For SSp-bfd, L5 and L6 dominated the contralateral input.
claims.source: In the case of SSp-bfd, L5 and L6 dominated the contralateral input (Figure 3C2, D2, L5 vs. L2/3 and L6 vs. L2/3, p < 0.01, one-way ANOVA, Tukey–Kramer multiple comparison correction)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of laminar dominance patterns for contralateral projections to SSp-bfd.

claims.claim: For SSp-bfd, L5 and L6 shared dominance with L2/3 only for the ipsilateral projection.
claims.source: and shared dominance with L2/3 only for the ipsilateral projection (Figure 3C1, D1, L5 vs. L2/3, p = 0.06; L6 vs. L2/3, p = 0.64, one-way ANOVA, Tukey–Kramer multiple comparison correction).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis showing no significant difference between L2/3, L5, and L6 for ipsilateral projections to SSp-bfd.

claims.claim: The majority of projection source areas display L6 dominance, followed by L5 with only a small fraction of areas exhibiting L2/3 dominance.
claims.source: When pooled across target areas, we find that the majority of projection source areas display L6 dominance, followed by L5 with only a small fraction of areas exhibiting L2/3 dominance (Figure 3E, p < 0.05, one-way ANOVA, Tukey–Kramer multiple comparison correction).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of laminar dominance patterns pooled across all target areas.

claims.claim: In primates, a predominance of incoming projection neurons from supragranular layers (L2/3) signifies a feedforward connection, whereas a higher proportion in infragranular layers (Layers 5 and 6) is considered to reflect a feedback projection.
claims.source: In primates, the laminar distribution of projection neurons has been used to interpret the degree to which corticocortical networks might be feedforward or feedback (Barone et al., 2000; Markov et al., 2014; Vezoli et al., 2021). A predominance of incoming projection neurons from supragranular layers (L2/3) signifies a feedforward connection, whereas a higher proportion in infragranular layers (Layers 5 and 6) is considered to reflect a feedback projection (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on established principles from prior anatomical studies in primates.

claims.claim: Cortical areas with a higher proportion of projection neurons in infragranular, compared to supragranular layers, are suggested to have a higher hierarchical rank.
claims.source: Additionally, cortical areas with a higher proportion of projection neurons in infragranular, compared to supragranular layers, are suggested to have a higher hierarchical rank (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on established principles from prior anatomical studies.

claims.claim: Using retrograde AAV-EF1a-H2B-EGFP, the hierarchical ranking of higher cortical visual areas is very similar to that previously shown.
claims.source: Using retrograde AAV-EF1a-H2B-EGFP and by detecting EGFP expression in the nuclei of projection neurons we find a very similar hierarchical ranking of the higher cortical visual areas as previously shown (Figure 4—figure supplement 1, D'Souza et al., 2022; Siegle et al., 2021; Yao et al., 2023).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of fILN-based hierarchy with prior studies using different methods.

claims.claim: Cortical input onto VISp, SSp-bfd, and MOp reflects predominantly a feedback organization, independent of the target area.
claims.source: Independent of the target area, the average fILN for both hemispheres indicates that cortical input onto VISp, SSp-bfd, and MOp reflects predominantly a feedback organization (Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by fILN values exceeding 0.5 for all target areas, indicating predominance of infragranular input.

claims.claim: The average fILN of the contralateral hemisphere is larger than the ipsilateral hemisphere across all injection targets.
claims.source: However, on average, and compared to the ipsilateral projection, the average fILN of the contralateral hemisphere is larger across all injection targets (Figure 4C, p < 0.05, one-sided paired t-test, respectively).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical comparison of fILN values between hemispheres for each target area.

claims.claim: The overall contralateral input appears more narrowly distributed in its degree of anatomical hierarchy, maintaining relatively high fILN values across all brain areas.
claims.source: Moreover, the overall contralateral input appears more narrowly distributed in its degree of anatomical hierarchy, maintaining relatively high fILN values across all brain areas (Figure 4C, D; fILN range ipsilateral: 0.42 ± 0.1 to 1.0 ± 0.0 vs. contralateral: 0.66 ± 0.07 to 1 ± 0).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of the range of fILN values between hemispheres.

claims.claim: There is a significant negative correlation between the areal fILN values on the ipsilateral side and the magnitude of the difference in the fILN of their contralateral counterpart.
claims.source: As a consequence, regardless of the target area, we found a significant negative correlation between the areal fILN values on the ipsilateral side and the magnitude of the difference in the fILN of their contralateral counterpart (Figure 4E, VISp: r = –0.71 ± 0.07, SSp-bfd: r = –0.7 ± 0.04, MOp: r = –0.77 ± 0.04, p < 0.05, Spearman correlation)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by Spearman correlation analysis showing negative relationships for all three target areas.

claims.claim: The ranking of contralateral hierarchy remained similar to that of the ipsilateral hierarchy.
claims.source: although the ranking of contralateral hierarchy remained similar to that of the ipsilateral hierarchy (Figure 4F, ipsi- vs. contralateral fILN: VISp: r = 0.74 ± 0.03, SSp-bfd: r = 0.63 ± 0.08, MOp: r = 0.63 ± 0.03, p < 0.05, Spearman correlation).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by Spearman correlation analysis showing positive relationships between ipsi- and contralateral fILN rankings.

claims.claim: There is feedforward input from VISp to SSp-bfd and feedback input from SSp-bfd to VISp within the ipsilateral hemisphere.
claims.source: In line with the classical view of reciprocal feedforward/feedback connectivity (Angelucci and Petreanu, 2023; Markov et al., 2014; Young et al., 2021) and in the case where we can directly compare the interconnectivity of two target sources within the ipsilateral hemisphere (VISp and SSp-bfd), we see feedforward input from VISp to SSp-bfd and feedback input from SSp-bfd to VISp (Figure 4E, Figure 4—figure supplement 2A, B, magenta and green arrows).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by fILN analysis showing reciprocal feedforward/feedback organization between VISp and SSp-bfd, consistent with prior studies.

claims.claim: All contralateral areas were found to provide predominantly feedback input.
claims.source: However, all contralateral areas were found to provide predominantly feedback input (Figure 4D–G, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by fILN analysis showing high values (>0.5) for contralateral projections from all areas.

claims.claim: In SSp-bfd, ipsilateral input from a subset of visual areas showed feedforward organization while contralateral input from the same areas showed feedback organization.
claims.source: These data also reveal unique instances, for example in SSp-bfd, where the ipsi- and contralateral input from a subset of visual areas showed opposing signatures in their anatomical organization. Ipsilateral mediating feedforward while contralateral providing feedback input (highlighted in red in Figure 4E, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by fILN analysis showing opposing hierarchical signatures for the same areas projecting from different hemispheres.

claims.claim: Within the ipsilateral hemisphere, anterogradely labeled sensory–motor module projections exhibit low hierarchy compared to lateral, medial and prefrontal modules.
claims.source: Within the ipsilateral hemisphere, anterogradely labeled sensory–motor module projections have been shown to exhibit low hierarchy compared to lateral, medial and prefrontal modules (Harris et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on prior anterograde tracing studies.

claims.claim: Using retrograde tracing and fILN measure, sensory-motor modules show lower hierarchy than prefrontal, medial, and lateral modules in both ipsilateral and contralateral hemispheres.
claims.source: Using retrograde tracing and our fILN measure we find this to be the case not only for the ipsilateral hemisphere but also for the contralateral hemisphere (Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by fILN analysis showing lower values for sensory-motor modules compared to other modules in both hemispheres.

claims.claim: Prefrontal, medial, and lateral modules show extremely similarly high levels of feedback from both hemispheres.
claims.source: Strikingly, ranking cortical modules according to their fILN values revealed extremely similarly high levels of feedback from prefrontal, medial, and lateral modules (pf-m-l) from both hemispheres.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by fILN analysis showing similar high values for these modules across hemispheres.

claims.claim: The fILN values for visual, auditory, and somatomotor (v-a-sm) modules were different across the two hemispheres with the contralateral hemisphere providing much stronger feedback.
claims.source: In contrast, the fILN values for visual, auditory, and somatomotor (v-a-sm) modules were different across the two hemispheres (Figure 5A, B) with the contralateral hemisphere providing much stronger feedback (Figure 5A, B, ipsilateral fILN 0.65 ± 0.02 vs. contralateral fILN 0.79 ± 0.01, p < 0.001, two-sided paired t-test).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical comparison of fILN values for sensory-motor modules between hemispheres.

claims.claim: The difference between the ipsi- and contralateral fILN was significantly larger for the v-a-sm compared to the pf-m-l modules when the data were partitioned according to the target areas.
claims.source: The difference between the ipsi- and contralateral fILN was also significantly larger for the v-a-sm compared to the pf-m-l modules when the data were partitioned according to the target areas (Figure 5C, p < 0.001, one-sided paired t-test).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical comparison of interhemispheric fILN differences between module groupings.

claims.claim: The global differences in the fILN between the two hemispheres are mainly due to hemispheric differences in the fILN between the v-a-sm modules.
claims.source: Moreover, these results suggest that the global differences in the fILN between the two hemispheres observed above are mainly due to hemispheric differences in the fILN between the v-a-sm modules.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the data showing larger interhemispheric differences for sensory-motor modules compared to other modules.

claims.claim: By pooling all areas within the three key sensory and motor modules for the contralateral side, there is a significant reduction in L2/3 neurons for all target areas.
claims.source: By pooling all areas (n = 24) within the three key sensory and motor modules for the contralateral side we observe a significant reduction in L2/3 neurons for all target areas (Figure 6B, ipsi- vs. contralateral L2/3 fractional counts: VISp 0.25 ± 0.02 vs. 0.15 ± 0.02, SSp-bfd 0.36 ± 0.02 vs. 0.22 ± 0.03, MOp 0.23 ± 0.01 vs. 0.1±0.01, p < 0.001, one-sided paired t-test)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical comparison of L2/3 fractional counts between hemispheres for sensory-motor modules.

claims.claim: There is a concomitant increase in L6 cells in VISp and SSp-bfd for contralateral projections from sensory-motor modules.
claims.source: and a concomitant increase in L6 cells in VISp and SSp-bfd (Figure 6B, ipsilateral vs. contralateral L6 fractional counts: VISp 0.38 ± 0.02 vs. 0.42 ± 0.01, SSp-bfd 0.24 ± 0.04 vs. 0.4 ± 0.01, p < 0.05, one-sided paired t-test).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical comparison of L6 fractional counts between hemispheres for VISp and SSp-bfd.

claims.claim: There was no change in the fraction of L5 neurons between the ipsi- and contralateral hemispheres for sensory-motor modules.
claims.source: We found there to be no change in the fraction of L5 neurons between the ipsi- and contralateral hemispheres (Figure 6B, ipsi- vs. contralateral L5 fractional counts: VISp 0.19 ± 0.02 vs. 0.21 ± 0.01, p = 0.38; SSp-bfd 0.27 ± 0.04 vs. 0.28 ± 0.01, p = 0.86; MOp 0.13 ± 0.02 vs. 0.12 ± 0.2, p = 0.24, two-sided paired t-test).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical comparison showing no significant difference in L5 fractional counts between hemispheres.

claims.claim: Depending on the target area, 30–60% of sensory-motor areas showed a dramatic reduction in the fraction of contralaterally labeled L2/3 neurons compared to their ipsilateral areal counterparts.
claims.source: Taking only those areas where we observed a significant change in the fraction of L2/3, L5, or L6 cells we found that, depending on the target area, 30–60% of sensory-motor areas showed a dramatic reduction in the fraction of contralaterally labeled L2/3 neurons compared to their ipsilateral areal counterparts.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of significant changes in laminar fractions between hemispheres for individual areas.

claims.claim: Between 30% and 50% of sensory-motor areas showed increases in contralateral L6 cells.
claims.source: In contrast, between 30% and 50% of areas showed increases in contralateral L6 cells.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of significant changes in L6 fractions between hemispheres for individual areas.

claims.claim: L5 showed on average little change since its fractional contribution both increased and decreased depending on the target area.
claims.source: On the other hand, L5 showed on average little change since its fractional contribution both increased and decreased depending on the target area (Figure 6D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by analysis showing bidirectional changes in L5 fractions across different target areas.

claims.claim: Increased fILN in the contralateral hemisphere is due to an increase in relative abundance of L6 CCs.
claims.source: These data show that increased fILN in the contralateral hemisphere is due to an increase in relative abundance of L6 CCs and indicates their key role in routing interhemispheric feedback.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the data showing increased L6 contributions and decreased L2/3 contributions in contralateral projections.

claims.claim: Excluding L5 or L6 from the fILN calculation results in significant changes in ipsilateral fILN values for cortical areas within the v-a-sm modules.
claims.source: First, by comparing the default ipsilateral fILN values for all cortical areas located within the v-a-sm modules to those when L5 or L6 was excluded, we observe significant changes in fILN (Figure 6E, p < 0.001, two-sided paired t-test, Bonferroni multiple comparison correction).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical comparison of fILN values with and without specific layers included.

claims.claim: The reduction in ipsi fILN was greatest when L6 was excluded compared to L5.
claims.source: Importantly, the reduction in ipsi fILN was greatest when L6 was excluded compared to L5 (Figure 6E, p < 0.05, one-sided paired t-test, Bonferroni multiple comparison correction).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical comparison of the magnitude of fILN reduction when excluding L5 versus L6.

claims.claim: Excluding L6 from the contralateral default network resulted in fILN values substantially lower than the default ipsilateral side.
claims.source: Excluding L6 from the contralateral default network actually had such a significant impact that the resultant fILN was substantially lower than the default ipsilateral side (Figure 6F, default fILN ipsilateral 0.65 ± 0.03 vs. fILN contra excluding L6 0.52 ± 0.05, p < 0.05, one-sided paired t-test, Bonferroni multiple comparison correction).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical comparison showing that removing L6 from contralateral calculations reduces fILN below ipsilateral baseline.

claims.claim: L6 exerts a major influence on the anatomical organization of cortical input onto VISp, SSp-bfd, and MOp and accounts for the differences in the feedback hierarchy observed within and between the two hemispheres.
claims.source: These data show that L6 exerts a major influence on the anatomical organization of cortical input onto VISp, SSp-bfd, and MOp and accounts for the differences in the feedback hierarchy observed within and between the two hemispheres.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the data showing that excluding L6 has the largest impact on fILN values and eliminates interhemispheric differences.

claims.claim: Both primary sensory and motor areas receive extensive input from the majority of areas located in the ipsilateral cortical hemisphere.
claims.source: By performing comprehensive bilateral cortical circuit mapping onto VISp, SSp-bfd, and MOp we find that both primary sensory and motor areas receive extensive input from the majority of areas not only located in the ipsilateral (Ährlund-Richter et al., 2019; Brown et al., 2021; Hafner et al., 2019; Muñoz-Castañeda et al., 2021; Sun et al., 2019; Yao et al., 2023) but also contralateral cortical hemisphere (Goulas et al., 2017; Yao et al., 2023).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the current study's data and is consistent with prior studies.

claims.claim: Both primary sensory and motor areas receive extensive input from the majority of areas located in the contralateral cortical hemisphere.
claims.source: By performing comprehensive bilateral cortical circuit mapping onto VISp, SSp-bfd, and MOp we find that both primary sensory and motor areas receive extensive input from the majority of areas not only located in the ipsilateral (Ährlund-Richter et al., 2019; Brown et al., 2021; Hafner et al., 2019; Muñoz-Castañeda et al., 2021; Sun et al., 2019; Yao et al., 2023) but also contralateral cortical hemisphere (Goulas et al., 2017; Yao et al., 2023).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the current study's data and is consistent with prior studies.

claims.claim: The identity, hierarchical rank and relative projection weights of input areas is highly conserved across the two hemispheres with only a few exceptions.
claims.source: With only a few exceptions, we find that the identity, hierarchical rank and relative projection weights of input areas is highly conserved across the two hemispheres.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analyses showing strong relationships between ipsi- and contralateral projections.

claims.claim: The contralateral lateral module displays a stronger connection onto VISp, SSp-bfd and MOp compared to the ipsilateral module, which may be a unique but generalizable feature of interhemispheric connectivity.
claims.source: One such exception relates to the contralateral lateral module whose composite cortical areas, compared to the ipsilateral module, display a stronger connection onto VISp (Yao et al., 2023), SSp-bfd and MOp indicating it may be a unique but generalizable feature of interhemispheric connectivity.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data showing increased contralateral lateral module contributions across all three target areas, with one citation to prior work.

claims.claim: Earlier studies indicate that input from the other hemisphere onto a given area arises primarily and almost exclusively from the same contralateral area.
claims.source: Earlier studies indicate that input from the other hemisphere onto a given area arises primarily and almost exclusively from the same contralateral area (Fenlon and Richards, 2015; Yorke and Caviness, 1975; Zhou et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on prior anatomical studies.

claims.claim: Heterotopic connections are a prominent anatomical feature of the interhemispheric network.
claims.source: While we find many labeled cells in the contralateral target area, our data indicate that heterotopic connections are a prominent anatomical feature of the interhemispheric network (Goulas et al., 2017; Swanson et al., 2017; Szczupak et al., 2023; Yao et al., 2023).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the current study's data showing extensive labeling outside homotopic areas and is consistent with recent studies.

claims.claim: For both primary sensory areas the majority of the contralateral input comes from heterotopic areas located within target areas' home module followed by areas located within most of the remaining modules.
claims.source: For both primary sensory areas the majority of the contralateral input comes from heterotopic areas located within target areas' home module followed by areas located within most of the remaining modules.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of the modular distribution of contralateral projections.

claims.claim: MOp receives very little input from areas relating to medial, visual, and auditory modules.
claims.source: In contrast, MOp appears to receive very little input from areas relating to medial, visual, and auditory modules.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data showing minimal fractional counts from these modules to MOp.

claims.claim: Neurons projecting from the contralateral hemisphere are believed to primarily reside within L2/3 and to a lesser extent in L5.
claims.source: Neurons projecting from the contralateral hemisphere are believed to primarily reside within L2/3 and to a lesser extent in L5 (Fame et al., 2011; Pal et al., 2024; Ramos et al., 2008; Yorke and Caviness, 1975).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on prior anatomical studies.

claims.claim: From an anatomical organization perspective, predominant L2/3 projections would be designated as predominantly feedforward.
claims.source: From an anatomical organization perspective, this would be designated as predominantly feedforward (Markov et al., 2014; Markov et al., 2013a; Markov and Kennedy, 2013b).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on established principles from prior studies.

claims.claim: L2/3 dominates the projection from the least number of cortical areas.
claims.source: We however find that L2/3 dominates the projection from the least number of cortical areas.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of laminar dominance patterns across cortical areas.

claims.claim: L6 emerges as a major source of both the intra- and especially the interhemispheric projection for the majority of areas.
claims.source: Rather for the majority of areas, L6 emerges as a major source of both the intra- and especially the interhemispheric projection (Liang et al., 2021; Olavarria and Van Sluyters, 1983; Yao et al., 2023), especially for VISp and MOp.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the current study's data and is consistent with some prior studies.

claims.claim: The combined dominance of L5 and L6 projecting neurons indicates that the vast majority of cortical projections to primary sensory and motor regions are feedback in nature.
claims.source: The combined dominance of L5 and L6 projecting neurons shown here indicates that the vast majority of cortical projections to primary sensory and motor regions are feedback in nature.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the laminar distribution data showing predominance of infragranular layers.

claims.claim: Chemical or protein-based anterograde and retrograde tracers such as Cholera toxin subunit B (CTB) have low transduction efficiency compared to recently developed retrograde viruses.
claims.source: Chemical or protein-based anterograde and retrograde tracers such as Cholera toxin subunit B (CTB) have been widely used but have low transduction efficiency (Saleeba et al., 2019; Weiler et al., 2024) compared to recently developed retrograde viruses (Tervo et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on prior technical comparisons of tracing methods.

claims.claim: Not all cell types are accessible using cre-driver lines, as is the case for L6 CCs.
claims.source: Second, mouse cre lines are a common tool for targeting specific cells in specific layers (Bortone et al., 2014; Harris et al., 2019; Yao et al., 2023). However, as is the case for L6 CCs (Vélez-Fort et al., 2014), not all cell types are accessible using cre-driver lines.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on prior studies documenting limitations of cre-driver lines.

claims.claim: Previous tracing studies appear biased toward upper layers of the injection area.
claims.source: In our study, we targeted all cell types located throughout all laminae within the target area that is in contrast to previous tracing studies that appear biased toward upper layers of the injection area (Adaikkan et al., 2022; Chovsepian et al., 2017; Massé et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on comparison with prior tracing studies.

claims.claim: The observed predominance of L6 labeling is unlikely to be attributed to labeling bias since viral injections effectively covered all cortical layers and excluded the white matter.
claims.source: It also seems unlikely that the observed predominance of L6 labeling revealed here can be attributed to labeling bias since our viral injections effectively covered all cortical layers and excluded the white matter.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on analysis of injection site coverage and exclusion criteria.

claims.claim: Multiple contra- and ipsilateral areas exhibit significant labeling in L2/3 and/or 5.
claims.source: Moreover, multiple contra- and ipsilateral areas exhibit significant labeling in L2/3 and/or 5
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by laminar distribution data showing labeling across multiple layers.

claims.claim: Prior studies using non-viral tracers such as CTB or Fluorogold have similarly reported a dominance of L6 projection neurons in specific pathways (e.g. SSp-bfd → VISp).
claims.source: and prior studies using non-viral tracers such as CTB or Fluorogold have similarly reported a dominance of L6 projection neurons in the same specific pathways (e.g. SSp-bfd → VISp, Bieler et al., 2017; Weiler et al., 2024) as those revealed here using a retro-AAV-based approach.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on prior studies using different tracing methods that found similar results.

claims.claim: The fILN metric effectively ranks higher visual areas consistent with the anatomical organization derived from axon termination patterns, retrograde rabies tracing, and physiological experiments.
claims.source: Here, we demonstrate in mice that the fILN metric effectively ranks higher visual areas that is consistent with the anatomical organization derived from axon termination patterns, as well as retrograde rabies tracing (D'Souza et al., 2022; Harris et al., 2019; Yao et al., 2023) and physiological experiments that describe functional hierarchy in mice (D'Souza et al., 2022; Jia et al., 2022; Siegle et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of fILN-based rankings with prior anatomical and physiological studies.

claims.claim: The fILN-based area ranking reveals a global organization largely consistent with the hierarchical ranking of cortical areas based on anterograde labeling.
claims.source: By applying fILN-based area ranking cortex-wide, we uncover a global organization that is largely consistent with the hierarchical ranking of cortical areas based on anterograde labeling (Harris et al., 2019), placing sensory–motor modules at the bottom and lateral, medial, and prefrontal modules at the top of cortical hierarchy.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of fILN-based rankings with prior anterograde tracing studies.

claims.claim: The fILN metric can serve as a continuous parameter whose ranking may be used as an estimate of feedforward and feedback hierarchy for understanding cortical connectivity.
claims.source: Our data therefore demonstrate that the fILN metric can serve as a continuous parameter whose ranking may be used as an estimate of feedforward and feedback hierarchy for understanding cortical connectivity.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the validation of fILN against prior anatomical and physiological measures of hierarchy.

claims.claim: Feedforward projections are typically characterized as 'drivers' while feedback projections are seen as 'modulators' of neuronal activity.
claims.source: Typically, feedforward projections are characterized as 'drivers' while feedback projections are seen as 'modulators' of neuronal activity (Markov et al., 2013a).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on established concepts from prior studies.

claims.claim: VISp, SSp-bfd, and MOp mostly receive feedback from the ipsilateral cortex.
claims.source: Our anatomical data reveal that VISp, SSp-bfd, and MOp mostly receive feedback from the ipsilateral cortex.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by fILN analysis showing predominance of infragranular input.

claims.claim: The predominance of feedback projections suggests a modulatory role rather than driving input onto primary cortical areas.
claims.source: The predominance of feedback projections suggests a modulatory role rather than driving input onto these primary cortical areas.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the anatomical data showing feedback dominance combined with established concepts about feedback function.

claims.claim: The pairwise intra-hemispheric connectivity between VISp and SSp-bfd aligns well with historical theories of cortical hierarchy suggesting that feedforward connections are typically complemented by reciprocal feedback connections.
claims.source: From our data, the pairwise intra-hemispheric connectivity between VISp and SSp-bfd aligns well with historical theories of cortical hierarchy, which suggest that feedforward connections are typically complemented by reciprocal feedback connections, at least within the ipsilateral hemisphere (Angelucci and Petreanu, 2023; Felleman and Van Essen, 1991; Markov et al., 2013a; Young et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the current study's data showing reciprocal feedforward/feedback organization and is consistent with prior theories.

claims.claim: Ipsilateral primary and higher visual cortical areas provide cross-modal feedforward input onto SSp-bfd.
claims.source: Our data also reveal a notable exception that appears to involve ipsilateral primary and higher visual cortical areas providing cross-modal feedforward input onto SSp-bfd.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by fILN analysis showing low values for ipsilateral visual area projections to SSp-bfd.

claims.claim: Input from visual areas on the contralateral side to SSp-bfd are feedback in their organization.
claims.source: On the other hand, input from the same areas on the contralateral side are feedback in their organization as one might expect to observe for higher-order areas.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by fILN analysis showing high values for contralateral visual area projections to SSp-bfd.

claims.claim: Regardless of the target area, contralateral projections are predominantly feedback, suggesting that the conventional rule of reciprocally feedforward and feedback projections does not apply for interhemispheric input to primary areas VISp, SSp-bfd, or MOp.
claims.source: The fact that, regardless of the target area, contralateral projections are predominantly feedback suggests that the conventional rule of reciprocally feedforward and feedback projections does not apply for interhemispheric input at least to primary areas VISp, SSp-bfd, or MOp.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the data showing uniformly high fILN values for contralateral projections.

claims.claim: Due to their dominant feedback bias, contralateral inputs may act as modulators of cortical activity within their ipsilateral target regions.
claims.source: Due to their dominant feedback bias, contralateral inputs may act as modulators of cortical activity within their ipsilateral target regions (Innocenti et al., 2022; Markov et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: The claim is speculative, inferred from the anatomical feedback organization and supported by prior concepts about feedback function.

claims.claim: Inactivation of contralateral somatosensory areas in monkeys increases the receptive field size in the ipsilateral somatosensory area, suggesting a loss of modulatory contralateral input.
claims.source: For instance, inactivation of contralateral somatosensory areas in monkeys increases the receptive field size in the ipsilateral somatosensory area, suggesting a loss of modulatory contralateral input (Clarey et al., 1996).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on prior physiological studies in primates.

claims.claim: Contralateral auditory projections act to sharpen frequency tuning in its ipsilateral counterpart.
claims.source: Moreover, contralateral auditory projections act to sharpen frequency tuning in its ipsilateral counterpart (Slater and Isaacson, 2020)
claims.evidence: The claim is based on prior physiological studies.

claims.claim: Activation of contralateral visual projections strongly modulates visual cortical responses in the binocular zone of VISp.
claims.source: and activation of contralateral visual projections strongly modulates visual cortical responses in the binocular zone of VISp (Zhao et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on prior physiological studies.

claims.claim: Prior studies on contralateral projections focused purely on homotopic areas while the functions of heterotopic areas largely remain elusive.
claims.source: However, these studies focused purely on homotopic areas while the functions of heterotopic areas largely remain elusive.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on assessment of the scope of prior physiological studies.

claims.claim: L6 CCs not only integrate input from and output to its local cortical column but also receive substantial thalamic input, at least in sensory areas.
claims.source: L6 CCs not only integrate input from and output to its local cortical column (Vélez-Fort et al., 2014) but also receive substantial thalamic input, at least in sensory areas (Crandall et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on prior anatomical and physiological studies of L6 CC connectivity.

claims.claim: Responses of L6 CCs to external stimuli temporally precedes those in other cortical layers.
claims.source: Moreover, responses of L6 CCs to external stimuli temporally precedes those in other cortical layers (Egger et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on prior physiological studies of L6 CC response timing.

claims.claim: L6 CCs are ideal candidates to rapidly relay information to other cortical areas thereby providing feedback modulation, suggestive of predictive coding, or the transmission of efference copy.
claims.source: Thus, L6 CCs are ideal candidates to rapidly relay information to other cortical areas thereby providing feedback modulation (Weiler et al., 2024), suggestive of predictive coding (Rao and Ballard, 1999), or the transmission of efference copy (Latash, 2021; Vallortigara, 2021; von Holst and Mittelstaedt, 1950).
claims.evidence: The claim is speculative, inferred from the anatomical and temporal properties of L6 CCs combined with theoretical frameworks.

claims.claim: Only brains that had viral transduction levels of the white matter below 0.1% of the total bolus volume were included in the analysis.
claims.source: Importantly, only brains that had viral transduction levels of the white matter below 0.1% of the total bolus volume were included (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
claims.evidence: The claim describes an inclusion criterion for the study.

claims.claim: Feedforward connections typically carry sensory input toward areas higher in cortical hierarchy where more complex processing occurs.
claims.source: In the case of sensory processing, feedforward connections typically carry sensory input toward areas higher in cortical hierarchy where more complex processing occurs (Felleman and Van Essen, 1991; Mumford, 1992; Rockland and Pandya, 1979; Siegle et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on established principles from prior studies of cortical hierarchy.

claims.claim: Cortical feedback typically originates in higher-order areas and projects back to brain areas of lower hierarchical rank.
claims.source: Conversely, cortical feedback typically originates in higher-order areas and projects back to brain areas of lower hierarchical rank (Felleman and Van Essen, 1991; Markov et al., 2014; Rockland and Pandya, 1979).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on established principles from prior studies of cortical hierarchy.

claims.claim: Feedback pathways are believed to be crucial for modulating sensory processing, enhancing signal fidelity, integrating contextual information, and forming predictions.
claims.source: These pathways are believed to be crucial for modulating sensory processing (Weiler et al., 2024), enhancing signal fidelity (Xu et al., 2012), integrating contextual information (Zhang et al., 2014), and forming predictions (Keller and Mrsic-Flogel, 2018; Leinweber et al., 2017; Rao and Ballard, 1999).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on prior physiological and theoretical studies of feedback function.

claims.claim: Retrograde tracing and physiological analysis in the visual cortical system of primates indicate that supragranular layers are the main source of feedforward projections while infragranular layers are the main source of feedback input.
claims.source: For instance, retrograde tracing (Markov et al., 2014) and physiological analysis (Bastos et al., 2015; Buffalo et al., 2011) in the visual cortical system of primates indicate that supragranular layers are the main source of feedforward projections while infragranular layers are the main source of feedback input.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on prior anatomical and physiological studies in primates.

claims.claim: The ratio of supra- to infragranular layer projections has been used to reveal the anatomical basis of visual cortical hierarchy in primates and mice.
claims.source: Moreover, the ratio of supra- to infragranular layer projections has been used to reveal the anatomical basis of visual cortical hierarchy in primates and mice (Barone et al., 2000; D'Souza et al., 2022; Markov et al., 2014; Yao et al., 2023).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on prior anatomical studies using laminar projection patterns to define hierarchy.

claims.claim: It remains unknown how functional cortical hierarchy within the ipsilateral hemisphere is combined with or reflects the organization of input from the contralateral hemisphere.
claims.source: While it is established that functional cortical hierarchy (at least in the visual system) reflects the laminar organization of cortical input within the ipsilateral hemisphere, it remains unknown how this is combined or even reflects the organization of input from the contralateral hemisphere.
claims.evidence: The claim identifies a gap in current knowledge that the study addresses.

claims.claim: To date there remains no cortex-wide anatomical analysis that investigates the nature of circuit hierarchy onto a given area that arises from both hemispheres.
claims.source: More specifically, to date there remains no cortex-wide anatomical analysis that investigates the nature of circuit hierarchy onto a given area that arises from both hemispheres.
claims.evidence: The claim identifies a gap in current knowledge that the study addresses.

claims.claim: Which cortical layers are responsible for the establishment of the intra- versus the interhemispheric cortical hierarchy is not understood.
claims.source: Also, which cortical layers are responsible for the establishment of the intra- versus the interhemispheric cortical hierarchy is not understood.
claims.evidence: The claim identifies a gap in current knowledge that the study addresses.

claims.claim: The corpus callosum is thought to coordinate function across the brain.
claims.source: Rather, they are connected by commissural fibers, most notably the corpus callosum which is thought to coordinate function across the brain (Gazzaniga, 2000; Innocenti et al., 2022; Ocklenburg and Guo, 2024; Zhou et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on prior studies of interhemispheric connectivity.

results.result: Primary sensory and motor cortices receive extensive bilateral cortical input with approximately 80% ipsilateral and 20% contralateral, showing substantial symmetry in relative contribution and areal identity across hemispheres.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C12 collectively demonstrate bilateral cortical input patterns with strong statistical support. The 80/20 ipsilateral/contralateral distribution (C1), high correlation coefficients between hemispheres (C11: R²=0.74-0.83), and extensive areal coverage (C8-C9) provide converging evidence. Statistical testing with appropriate corrections supports the symmetry claims (C12).

results.result: Layer 6 corticocortical cells (L6 CCs) dominate cortical projections to primary sensory and motor areas, with L6 being the predominant source layer rather than L2/3.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C18-C23, C62-C63 provide consistent evidence for L6 dominance through laminar distribution analysis with statistical testing (ANOVA with multiple comparison correction). The finding contradicts prior expectations (C60-C61) but is supported by quantitative data across all target areas and validated against potential technical artifacts (C68-C70).

results.result: Contralateral projections exhibit stronger feedback organization than ipsilateral projections, with higher and more narrowly distributed fILN values across all target areas.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C27-C31, C33 demonstrate interhemispheric differences in hierarchical organization through fILN analysis. Statistical comparisons show significantly higher contralateral fILN values (C28: p<0.05), narrower distribution (C29), and negative correlation with ipsilateral values (C30: r=-0.70 to -0.77). The consistency across all three target areas strengthens the conclusion.

results.result: The interhemispheric difference in hierarchical organization is largest for sensory-motor modules compared to prefrontal-medial-lateral modules, driven by decreased L2/3 and increased L6 contributions in contralateral projections.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C36-C47 provide detailed mechanistic evidence for module-specific interhemispheric differences. Statistical comparisons show significantly larger fILN differences for sensory-motor modules (C38-C39: p<0.001), with specific laminar changes quantified (C41-C42: decreased L2/3, increased L6). The convergence of modular analysis (C36-C40) and laminar analysis (C41-C47) strongly supports the conclusion.

results.result: L6 exerts the major influence on anatomical hierarchy, with its exclusion from fILN calculations producing the largest reductions and eliminating interhemispheric differences.
results.evaluation: Claims C48-C51 demonstrate L6's critical role through layer exclusion analysis with appropriate statistical testing (Bonferroni correction). The finding that excluding L6 from contralateral calculations reduces fILN below ipsilateral baseline (C50: p<0.05) provides strong evidence. However, this is an analytical manipulation rather than experimental intervention, limiting causal interpretation.

results.result: Retrogradely labeled projection neurons are predominantly excitatory (>99% non-GAD+) and L6 projections are corticocortical rather than corticothalamic (non-NTSR1+).
results.evaluation: Claims C6-C7 are supported by confocal imaging with appropriate cell-type markers (GAD for interneurons, NTSR1 for L6 corticothalamic cells). The >99% non-overlap with GAD+ cells and complete non-overlap with NTSR1+ cells provide clear evidence. However, sample size for confocal validation is not specified, and validation was performed on subset of animals.

results.result: Cortical projections show modular organization with VISp dominated by visual module input, SSp-bfd and MOp by somatomotor module input, and MOp receiving minimal input from visual, auditory, and medial modules.
results.evaluation: Claims C13-C17 demonstrate modular organization through fractional count analysis with statistical testing. The modular framework (C13) is based on prior work (Harris et al., 2019), and current data show clear module-specific patterns (C14-C16: p<0.001). The contralateral lateral module bias (C17) is marginally significant (p=0.05) but consistent across targets.

results.result: The fILN metric effectively ranks cortical hierarchy in mice, consistent with prior anatomical and physiological measures, and can serve as a continuous parameter for estimating feedforward/feedback organization.
results.evaluation: Claims C24-C26, C71-C73 validate the fILN approach through comparison with established primate principles (C24-C25) and prior mouse studies (C26, C71-C72). The consistency across multiple methodologies (anterograde tracing, rabies tracing, physiology) supports the metric's validity. However, the claim that fILN 'can serve' as a hierarchy metric (C73) is somewhat circular since it's validated against other anatomical measures rather than independent functional criteria.

results.result: Ipsilateral VISp-SSp-bfd connectivity shows reciprocal feedforward/feedback organization, but contralateral projections are uniformly feedback, with some visual areas showing opposing hierarchical signatures across hemispheres.
results.evaluation: Claims C32, C34, C77-C80 demonstrate complex interhemispheric organizational patterns. The reciprocal ipsilateral organization (C32) aligns with classical theories, while uniform contralateral feedback (C33, C80) represents a novel finding. The opposing signatures for visual areas projecting to SSp-bfd (C34, C78-C79) are particularly interesting but based on fILN analysis alone without functional validation.

results.result: Primary sensory and motor areas receive extensive heterotopic input from both hemispheres, with highly conserved identity and projection weights across hemispheres, except for enhanced contralateral lateral module connectivity.
results.evaluation: Claims C52-C55, C57-C59 demonstrate extensive heterotopic connectivity challenging prior views (C56). The conservation of projection patterns (C54) is supported by correlation analyses (C11), while the lateral module exception (C55) is consistent across targets. The heterotopic finding (C57) is supported by current data and consistent with recent literature.

results.result: The vast majority of cortical projections to primary sensory and motor regions are feedback in nature, suggesting a modulatory rather than driving role.
results.evaluation: Claims C64, C75-C76 synthesize the laminar and hierarchical findings to infer functional roles. The predominance of infragranular (L5/L6) projections (C64) is well-supported by data, and the inference of modulatory function (C76) is reasonable based on established principles (C74). However, this remains an anatomical inference without direct functional validation.

results.result: The observed L6 dominance is unlikely due to technical bias, as viral injections covered all layers, excluded white matter, and findings are consistent with prior studies using different tracers.
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C70 address potential technical concerns through multiple lines of evidence: injection coverage analysis (C68, C89), comparison with prior methods (C65, C70), and observation of labeling in other layers (C69). The convergence with CTB/Fluorogold studies (C70) strengthens the conclusion. However, the comparison with prior studies is limited to specific pathways.

results.result: Contralateral inputs may act as modulators of ipsilateral cortical activity, as suggested by prior physiological studies showing modulatory effects in sensory areas.
results.evaluation: Claims C81-C85 propose functional interpretations based on anatomical feedback organization and prior physiological studies. While the anatomical data support feedback organization (C4, C27-C28), the functional claim (C81) is speculative and marked as such. Prior studies (C82-C84) support modulatory roles but focused on homotopic connections, leaving heterotopic function unclear (C85).

results.result: L6 CCs are positioned to rapidly relay information for feedback modulation, predictive coding, or efference copy transmission based on their connectivity and temporal response properties.
results.evaluation: Claims C86-C88 propose functional roles for L6 CCs based on prior studies of their connectivity (C86) and temporal properties (C87). However, the specific functional claims (C88) are explicitly speculative and not tested in the current study. The anatomical findings support L6 CCs as a major pathway but don't directly demonstrate the proposed functions.

results.result: Only brains with white matter viral transduction below 0.1% of total bolus volume were included in analysis.
results.evaluation: Claim C89 describes a clear inclusion criterion with quantitative threshold. This is supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 2B showing the measurement. This represents appropriate quality control for retrograde tracing experiments.

results.result: Prior work established principles of feedforward/feedback organization and cortical hierarchy based on laminar patterns, but interhemispheric organization and layer-specific contributions remained unknown.
results.evaluation: Claims C90-C98 accurately summarize prior knowledge and identify gaps addressed by the study. The established principles (C90-C94) are well-cited, and the identified gaps (C95-C97) are legitimate. This provides appropriate context for the study's contributions.

results.result: The study demonstrates substantial bilateral symmetry in cortical projections to primary sensory and motor areas. While approximately 80% of projection neurons are ipsilateral and 20% contralateral, there is strong correlation (R² = 0.64-0.83) between ipsilateral and contralateral fractional counts, with the identity and relative projection weights of input areas highly conserved across hemispheres.
results.evaluation: All three reviewers explicitly affirm these findings. Reviewer 1 states 'there is substantial symmetry between the two hemispheres regarding the areas sending projections,' Reviewer 2 notes 'the relative areal distribution of contralateral inputs followed the distribution of corresponding ipsilateral inputs,' and Reviewer 3 confirms 'considerable bilateral symmetry in the areas providing cortico-cortical inputs.' The evidence is described as 'compelling' with 'rigorous analyses.'

results.result: Layer 6 corticocortical cells (L6 CCs) emerge as the dominant source of both ipsilateral and especially contralateral projections to primary sensory and motor areas, contrasting with prior beliefs that L2/3 neurons dominate contralateral projections. L6 dominated projections for VISp and MOp in both hemispheres, while for SSp-bfd, L5 and L6 dominated contralateral input but shared dominance with L2/3 ipsilaterally.
results.evaluation: All reviewers explicitly support this finding as a major contribution. Reviewer 2 states 'The largest proportion of inputs originated from layer 6a cells, and this layer 6 dominance was more pronounced for contralateral than ipsilateral inputs' and notes these 'results contrast earlier studies which suggested that contralateral inputs...from L2/3 neurons.' Reviewer 3 confirms 'a larger proportion of inputs from contralateral areas originated from deeper layers (L5 and L6).' The reviewers describe the data as 'well-supported' and 'carefully analyzed.'

results.result: Contralateral projections exhibit predominantly feedback organization with higher fILN values than ipsilateral projections across all target areas. All contralateral areas provide predominantly feedback input, and this feedback dominance is more pronounced and narrowly distributed compared to ipsilateral projections, suggesting that conventional reciprocal feedforward/feedback rules do not apply to interhemispheric connections.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly affirm this as a key finding. Reviewer 1 states 'contra-hemispheric projections had more inputs from layer 6 neurons than ipsi-projecting ones' and notes this 'suggests that these connections provide predominantly feedback inputs.' Reviewer 2 confirms 'layer 6 dominance was more pronounced for contralateral than ipsilateral inputs, which suggests that these connections provide predominantly feedback inputs.' The conclusions are described as 'well-supported by the data and analysis.'

results.result: The magnitude of interhemispheric differences in hierarchical organization is largest for sensory-motor modules compared to prefrontal-medial-lateral modules. While prefrontal, medial, and lateral modules show similarly high feedback levels from both hemispheres, visual-auditory-somatomotor modules show significantly different fILN values across hemispheres, with contralateral providing much stronger feedback.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept this modular analysis without critique. Reviewer 2 notes the study revealed 'several hundred thousand inputs into each region...dominated in number by connections within cortical sub-networks (e.g. anatomical modules)' and that 'within-module connections...ipsilateral connections were much more feed-forward than contralateral.' The analysis is described as part of the 'carefully analyzed' and 'well-supported' results.

results.result: The increased feedback hierarchy in contralateral projections is mechanistically driven by a significant reduction in L2/3 neurons and concomitant increase in L6 cells, particularly within sensory-motor modules. Excluding L6 from fILN calculations eliminates interhemispheric differences and reduces contralateral fILN below ipsilateral baseline, demonstrating L6's key role in establishing interhemispheric feedback hierarchy.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly support this mechanistic finding. Reviewer 2 states 'these results provide valuable data supporting a view of interhemispheric connectivity in which layer 6 neurons play an important role in providing modulatory feedback.' The layer-specific analysis is part of the 'state-of-the-art anatomical methods' that are 'very effectively presented and carefully analyzed' according to Reviewer 3.

results.result: Primary sensory and motor areas receive extensive input from almost all cortical areas in both hemispheres, with heterotopic connections being a prominent feature. VISp receives input dominated by the visual module, SSp-bfd and MOp by the somatomotor module, while MOp receives minimal input from visual, auditory, and medial modules.
results.evaluation: Reviewers affirm the comprehensive nature of these findings. Reviewer 2 notes 'Their analysis revealed several hundred thousand inputs into each region, with inputs originating from almost all cortical regions.' Reviewer 3 states the study 'fills in an important gap in the field' and 'should be of great utility and an important reference for future studies on inter hemispheric interactions.' No concerns are raised about these connectivity patterns.

results.result: The contralateral lateral module displays stronger connections to VISp, SSp-bfd, and MOp compared to its ipsilateral counterpart, driven primarily by temporal association area (TEa) and ectorhinal cortex (ECT), representing a potentially unique and generalizable feature of interhemispheric connectivity.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept this finding as part of the overall pattern of bilateral symmetry with specific exceptions. Reviewer 2 notes the study provides 'many novel insights on the similarities and differences of inputs from the two hemispheres,' implicitly accepting documented exceptions. No reviewer challenges this specific finding.

results.result: Within the ipsilateral hemisphere, VISp and SSp-bfd show reciprocal feedforward/feedback connectivity consistent with classical hierarchical theories. However, unique instances exist where ipsilateral visual areas provide feedforward input to SSp-bfd while the same contralateral areas provide feedback, demonstrating opposing hierarchical signatures.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 explicitly acknowledges this finding, stating 'The study finds that while ipsi- projections from visual cortex to barrel cortex are feedforward given its fILN values, those from the contralateral visual cortex are feedback instead. This is now acknowledged in the revised discussion.' This indicates reviewer acceptance of the finding after discussion clarification.

results.result: The fILN metric effectively ranks cortical areas in a hierarchy consistent with prior anatomical (anterograde tracing) and physiological studies, validating its use as a continuous parameter for estimating feedforward and feedback hierarchy in cortical connectivity.
results.evaluation: Reviewers implicitly accept the fILN methodology through their positive evaluation of the overall conclusions. Reviewer 1 states 'the conclusions are supported by rigorous analyses,' and Reviewer 2 notes 'The conclusions of this paper are well-supported by the data and analysis.' No reviewer questions the validity of the fILN metric or its interpretation.

results.result: The vast majority (>99%) of projection neurons are excitatory, non-overlapping with GAD-expressing interneurons, and L6 projection neurons are non-overlapping with NTSR1-expressing corticothalamic cells, confirming their identity as Layer 6 corticocortical cells (L6 CCs).
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not question the cell-type identification methods or conclusions. Reviewer 3 notes the study 'applies state-of-the-art anatomical methods' and the 'data is very effectively presented and carefully analyzed,' implicitly accepting the cell-type characterization as part of the rigorous methodology.

results.result: The observed L6 dominance is unlikely due to labeling bias since viral injections covered all cortical layers and excluded white matter, multiple areas show significant L2/3 and L5 labeling, and prior studies using different tracers (CTB, Fluorogold) reported similar L6 dominance in specific pathways.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not raise concerns about potential labeling bias. Reviewer 3 explicitly states 'I do not find any major weakness in the analyses or their interpretation,' and Reviewer 2 notes the study used 'state-of-the-art anatomical methods.' The methodological rigor is affirmed across reviews.

results.result: The predominance of feedback projections suggests contralateral inputs act as modulators rather than drivers of cortical activity in primary areas. L6 CCs are proposed as ideal candidates to rapidly relay information providing feedback modulation, potentially supporting predictive coding or efference copy transmission.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 explicitly states the results 'provide valuable data supporting a view of interhemispheric connectivity in which layer 6 neurons play an important role in providing modulatory feedback.' While these are interpretive claims, reviewers accept the functional implications drawn from the anatomical data without challenge.

comparisons.comparison: Perfect alignment on L6 dominance claims (C3, C18-C23, C62-C63). Both evaluations strongly support this finding as a major contribution, with peer reviewers explicitly noting it 'contrasts earlier studies' and OpenEval confirming it's 'supported by quantitative data across all target areas.' Both describe the evidence as compelling and well-analyzed.

Perfect alignment on cell-type identification (C6-C7). OpenEval supports the claims based on confocal imaging with appropriate markers, noting >99% non-overlap with GAD+ and complete non-overlap with NTSR1+. Peer reviewers implicitly accept this as part of 'state-of-the-art anatomical methods' without raising concerns.

Strong alignment on complex interhemispheric patterns (C32, C34, C77-C79). Both support the finding that visual-to-barrel projections show opposing ipsilateral/contralateral signatures. OpenEval notes this is 'particularly interesting but based on fILN analysis alone,' while peer reviewer explicitly acknowledges this after discussion clarification.

Strong alignment on interhemispheric hierarchical differences (C4, C27-C31, C33). Both evaluations support contralateral feedback dominance. OpenEval emphasizes statistical evidence (p<0.05, r=-0.70 to -0.77), while peer reviewers affirm this as a 'key finding' that is 'well-supported.' Peer review R3 also includes functional interpretation claims (C64, C75, C80) not in OpenEval R3.

Strong alignment on fILN validation (C26, C71-C73). Both support the metric's validity through comparison with prior studies. OpenEval notes some circularity in validation, while peer reviewers implicitly accept the methodology through positive evaluation of conclusions without questioning the metric.

Strong alignment on bilateral symmetry (C1-C2, C10-C12). Both evaluations support the 80/20 distribution and high correlation coefficients. OpenEval emphasizes statistical testing with corrections, while all three peer reviewers explicitly affirm findings with terms like 'compelling' and 'rigorous analyses.' Peer review also includes C54 (conservation of projection patterns) not in OpenEval R1.

Strong alignment on technical validation (C68-C70). Both evaluations support that L6 dominance is not a technical artifact. OpenEval details multiple validation approaches including injection coverage and comparison with CTB/Fluorogold studies. Peer reviewers affirm methodological rigor without raising labeling bias concerns.

Strong alignment on module-specific differences (C5, C36-C40). Both support sensory-motor module findings with significantly larger fILN differences. OpenEval emphasizes statistical evidence (p<0.001) and convergence of modular and laminar analysis. Peer reviewers accept this as part of 'carefully analyzed' results without critique.

Partial overlap on laminar mechanisms (C41-C47). OpenEval R4 addresses module-specific laminar changes, while peer R5 focuses on the broader mechanistic role of L6. Both support L6's importance in modulatory feedback. Peer R5 also includes layer exclusion analysis (C48-C51) that OpenEval addresses separately in R5.

Moderate alignment on L6 exclusion analysis (C48-C51). Both support this finding with appropriate statistical testing. OpenEval notes this is 'analytical manipulation rather than experimental intervention, limiting causal interpretation,' while peer reviewers accept it as supporting 'modulatory feedback' view. Peer R5 also includes laminar change claims (C41-C47) that OpenEval addresses in R4.

Moderate alignment on extensive connectivity patterns (C52-C53, C57-C59). Both support heterotopic connectivity findings. OpenEval emphasizes this challenges prior views and is consistent with recent literature. Peer reviewers note 'several hundred thousand inputs' from 'almost all cortical regions' and describe this as filling 'an important gap.' Peer R6 also includes areal coverage and modular claims (C8-C9, C14-C16) addressed elsewhere by OpenEval.

Partial overlap on modular organization (C14-C16). OpenEval R7 focuses on modular patterns with statistical testing, while peer R6 addresses broader connectivity patterns including modular aspects. Both support the findings without concerns. Peer R6 covers additional claims (C8-C9, C52-C53, C57-C59) not in OpenEval R7.

Minimal overlap on lateral module exception (C17). Both evaluations support this finding. OpenEval notes marginal significance (p=0.05) but consistency across targets. Peer reviewers accept this as part of documented exceptions to bilateral symmetry. Peer R7 also includes C55 not in OpenEval R7.

Partial overlap on functional interpretation (C76). OpenEval R11 addresses anatomical inference of modulatory function as reasonable but lacking direct functional validation. Peer R12 explicitly supports the modulatory feedback interpretation. Peer R12 also includes speculative claims (C81, C88) that OpenEval addresses separately as UNCERTAIN.

Minimal overlap on infragranular dominance and feedback (C64, C75). OpenEval R11 synthesizes laminar and hierarchical findings to infer functional roles, noting this is anatomical inference without functional validation. Peer R3 focuses on hierarchical differences with feedback interpretation, accepting functional implications. Peer R3 also includes C80 and hierarchical analysis claims not in OpenEval R11.

Divergent evaluation on functional speculation (C81). OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN, noting claims are 'speculative' with limited support from prior studies focused on homotopic connections. Peer reviewers rate as SUPPORTED, accepting the functional implications without challenge. This represents a key difference in how speculative functional claims are evaluated.

Divergent evaluation on L6 CC functional roles (C88). OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN, explicitly noting claims are 'speculative and not tested in the current study.' Peer reviewers rate as SUPPORTED, accepting the modulatory feedback interpretation. This represents another key difference in evaluating speculative functional claims beyond anatomical data.
